topic: Ollama coding agent: Qwen 3.8 27B mxfp8, OpenCode harness, sbx sandbox, context capped at 64K, on one laptop
title: Thirty-two gigabytes: the whole coding model on one laptop
hook_candidates: Thirty-two gigabytes. That's the whole model, on your laptop.
You've tried local models. Tonight one writes your code.
You've got one laptop. It can be your coding agent.
Three installs and your Mac runs a coding agent tonight.
A coding agent with no cloud, no key, no subscription.
Sixty-four thousand tokens. That's the cap that saves your laptop.
Your laptop isn't too small. The context window was uncapped.
Qwen 3.8 runs your agent. Ollama serves it. sbx cages it.
No API key. Your forty-eight-gigabyte Mac is the datacenter.
One developer front-paged the whole setup. Here's the stack.
narration_full: Thirty-two gigabytes of model, on your laptop. You've watched cloud coding agents work, but never pointed one at your own code. It's one download from Ollama, a free tool that serves local models. The model is Qwen's coding model, built for agent work. The trick is M X F P eight, a quantization. Weights are stored as eight-bit numbers, each block with its own scaling factor. A little accuracy buys a file one laptop holds. A model this size sounds like it belongs in a datacenter. Instead Ollama hands you qwen three point eight like a game download. Which means the model is the easy part of tonight. The setup around it is the real story. A coding agent is a harness: the model reads your files, runs commands, edits code. So you need a server, an agent, and a sandbox. Oh-lah-mah is already serving the model. OpenCode is the agent, open source, living in your terminal. And S B X is Docker's sandbox. Installing is boring, which is the point. Brew gives you the sandbox and the agent. The oh-lah-mah app comes from their site. Then one pull command downloads the model, all thirty-two gigabytes of it. Here's where your memory goes. The walkthrough's MacBook holds forty-eight gigabytes of memory, and everything shares it. The model parks in thirty-two of them. Context is the model's working memory, growing with every file opened. Picture a food truck: it rents its spot, and every order sits on the counter. A full counter never hurt a truck; it locks this laptop up. So the walkthrough caps context at sixty-five thousand five hundred thirty-six tokens. Left alone, oh-lah-mah hands out more context than your memory can pay for. The cap is the difference between a slow agent and a locked laptop. Also set reasoning effort, the model's hidden-thinking dial, to low for agent turns. The sandbox is the safety piece. S B X runs OpenCode in an isolated micro V M: own filesystem, own network. A hallucinated command wrecks the sandbox. Your files stay untouched. Keep a few gigabytes of memory aside for it, then S B X run starts the agent. The honest catch: it's slower than a cloud frontier model. Community speed reports swing wildly by chip, so treat any number as folklore. Some developers say skip Ollama for llama dot cpp. Nobody has shipped the benchmark that settles it. So that's tonight: three installs and a small config. One laptop becomes the whole datacenter: model, agent, and sandbox, no A P I key required.

analogy.vehicle: A food truck with a fixed parking spot: the model is the truck, memory the spot, context the counter space
analogy.mapping: the 32GB model rents its spot up front; every order (token of context) sits on the counter
analogy.limit: a food truck does not get slower as the counter fills, but memory pressure does lock the machine, which is why the 64K cap exists
